research_text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. What `java.security.KeyPair` governs, and what the finding can refer to

`java.security.KeyPair` is a final JCA holder for **one public key and one private key**. Oracle documents that it “does not enforce any security” and, once initialized, “should be treated like a `PrivateKey`.” Its constructor is `KeyPair(PublicKey publicKey, PrivateKey privateKey)` and stores references to those component objects; it does not accept a generator and does not document any generation/provenance check. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

Official API source:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html

Accordingly, **“no generator of the private key given to the KeyPair constructor was observed” is not a documented Java runtime event, exception, or `KeyPair` value**. The documented constructor value is simply its `privateKey` argument, of type `PrivateKey`. The supplied CrySL rule instead imposes an analysis predicate, `generatedPrivkey[privateKey]`, before construction. That predicate is a rule-level provenance fact; it is not part of the JCA `KeyPair` constructor contract. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

The relevant CrySL event is the constructor event:

> `c1: KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey);`

The rule requires `generatedPrivkey[privateKey]` and `generatedPubkey[publicKey]`; after the construction event it ensures `generatedKeypair[this, _]`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

The JCA API that documents generating a *new* key pair is `java.security.KeyPairGenerator`: `generateKeyPair()` generates a `KeyPair`, and the generator associates algorithm-specific parameters with generated keys. That is distinct from the `KeyPair` holder constructor. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

Source:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html

**Limit:** The CrySL file alone does not identify the detector implementation’s `UnsatisfiedConstraint` category, trace, analysis configuration, or why it reported the phrase “no generator … was observed.” Therefore, it is not possible from the supplied rule text to determine whether the report concerns a constructor argument’s unavailable provenance, an unmodeled library/framework boundary, or another analyzer-specific condition.

---

### 2. Official documented usage and remediation

#### What the official `KeyPair` API documents

Oracle documents the following:

* `KeyPair` is a simple holder for public/private key components and **does not enforce security**. It should be handled as a `PrivateKey` once initialized. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))
* `new KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey)` constructs the holder from supplied `PublicKey` and `PrivateKey` values. The constructor retains references to those objects; Oracle says that is safe because `Key` objects are immutable. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))
* `getPublic()` and `getPrivate()` return references to the respective components. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

The related `Key` contract states that keys are generally obtained through key generators, certificates, key stores, or other key-management classes; keys can also be obtained from key specifications through `KeyFactory`. It also warns that a serialized key may contain sensitive information that must not be exposed in untrusted environments. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

Source:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html

If an application is creating a new pair, `KeyPairGenerator` is the documented API for that task. Oracle recommends explicitly initializing a `KeyPairGenerator`, rather than relying on provider-specific defaults, because defaults may differ by provider and may change in a future version. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

#### What the official sources do **not** document

The official `KeyPair` documentation does **not** state that direct construction with `new KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey)` is improper, unsafe, deprecated, or prohibited. It also does **not** provide a `KeyPair`-specific “remediation” for a provenance finding, nor does it require that the component private key have been produced by `KeyPairGenerator`.

Therefore, an asserted remediation from direct construction to generation would be an analyzer/rule-policy conclusion, not a remediation prescribed by the `KeyPair` API documentation. The only documented recommendation found is the narrower `KeyPairGenerator` recommendation to explicitly initialize the generator **when a generator is used to create new key pairs**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

---

### 3. Compatibility, persisted/wire formats, version support, and migration

#### Platform/API support

`KeyPair` has been present since Java 1.1. The Java SE 8 and Java SE 17 API references document the same constructor signature, `KeyPair(PublicKey, PrivateKey)`, and the same two accessors. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

Oracle Java SE 8 source:  
https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyPair.html

#### Persisted Java serialization

`KeyPair` implements `Serializable`. The Java SE 17 serialized-form reference lists:

* `serialVersionUID`: `-7565189502268009837L`
* serialized fields: `privateKey` and `publicKey`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/serialized-form.html))

Source:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/serialized-form.html

This documents the Java serialization representation of `KeyPair`; it does **not** document a special serialization migration procedure related to changing how the component keys were obtained.

#### Wire/external key encodings

The `KeyPair` API itself does not specify a wire format. The component `Key` interface instead defines external encodings for keys: generally X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` for public keys and PKCS#8 `PrivateKeyInfo` for private keys, returned by `getEncoded()` where supported. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

Thus, official documentation separates:

* the in-memory `KeyPair` holder,
* Java object serialization of that holder, and
* external encodings of individual key objects.

It does not document a `KeyPair` wire encoding or a conversion/migration protocol triggered by using the holder constructor versus obtaining component keys through another documented mechanism. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

#### Documented migration path

No official migration path was found in the `KeyPair`, `Key`, or `KeyPairGenerator` documentation for this particular change in usage/provenance. In particular, the sources do not state that persisted `KeyPair` objects or external encodings must be transformed if component keys are sourced differently.

**Limit:** Compatibility of an actual stored object depends on the concrete `PublicKey`/`PrivateKey` implementation and provider, because `KeyPair` serializes references to those components. The cited `KeyPair` material does not establish cross-provider, cross-runtime, certificate, keystore, or protocol compatibility guarantees. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

---

### 4. Exact CrySL matching clause and condition

The supplied rule’s governing declaration is:

> `SPEC java.security.KeyPair`

Source:  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

The exact event clauses are:

> `c1: KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey);`  
> `Con := c1;`  
> `gpu1: retPublicKey = getPublic();`  
> `GetPubl := gpu1;`  
> `gpr1: retPrivateKey = getPrivate();`  
> `GetPriv := gpr1;` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

The declared parameter/object types are:

> `java.security.PrivateKey privateKey;`  
> `java.security.PublicKey publicKey;`  
> `java.security.PrivateKey retPrivateKey;`  
> `java.security.PublicKey retPublicKey;` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

Therefore, as stated by the rule text:

| Event alias | Named operation | Receiver/governed type declared by the rule | Parameter-list constraint in the event clause |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Con` | `KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey)` | `SPEC java.security.KeyPair` | Yes: two declared variables, `publicKey` and `privateKey`, whose declared types are `java.security.PublicKey` and `java.security.PrivateKey`. |
| `GetPubl` | `getPublic()` | `SPEC java.security.KeyPair` | Yes: zero arguments; a `java.security.PublicKey` result is assigned to `retPublicKey`. |
| `GetPriv` | `getPrivate()` | `SPEC java.security.KeyPair` | Yes: zero arguments; a `java.security.PrivateKey` result is assigned to `retPrivateKey`. |

The event-order expression is:

> `Con, (GetPubl | GetPriv)*` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

The conditions subsequently evaluated are exactly:

> `generatedPrivkey[privateKey];`  
> `generatedPubkey[publicKey];`  
> `noCallTo[Con] => generatedKeypair[this, _];` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

The consequent predicates are:

> `generatedKeypair[this, _] after Con;`  
> `generatedPubkey[retPublicKey] after GetPubl;`  
> `generatedPrivkey[retPrivateKey] after GetPriv;` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

#### Can this rule match a method that merely shares an API method name?

**At the rule-declaration level, no generic name-only target is declared.** The file scopes the rule as `SPEC java.security.KeyPair`; its getter events are within that specification, and its constructor event uses specifically typed `PublicKey` and `PrivateKey` variables. It does not declare a rule for every arbitrary method named `getPublic` or `getPrivate`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

**Source limit:** The CrySL text does not itself explain the analyzer’s method-resolution implementation, overload-resolution behavior, inheritance handling, or whether a particular tool version could emit a name-based false match. It supports the limited statement above about the rule’s declared scope and event syntax, but not a broader claim about the behavior of an unspecified detector implementation.
